Discharge Summary:

Patient: 46-year-old male

Admission date: [DATE]

Discharge date: [DATE]

Medical history: None reported except exertional dyspnea.

Chief complaint: Exertional dyspnea

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a chief complaint of exertional dyspnea. Physical examination revealed a systolic mitral murmur and a diastolic aortic murmur. TTE revealed a noncoronary SVA protruding into the mitral anterior leaflet, leading to moderate mitral regurgitation, severe aortic insufficiency, and a dilated aortic root. The ascending aorta measured 54-mm, and the left ventricular diastolic diameter was 75-mm, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 66%. No ventricular septal defect was detected. Coronary CTA showed no abnormalities or stenoses found in the coronary tree and the sac of the noncoronary SVA (measuring 36 × 47 × 51 mm) was protruding into the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. Surgery was performed via median sternotomy. The thickening of the wall of the tricuspid aortic valve and ascending aortic wall was consistent with inflammation. The patient underwent mitral valve and aortic valve replacement and replacement of the ascending aorta with an artificial vessel. Antibiotics were administered for 5 weeks. Follow-up TTE showed satisfactory functioning of both replaced valves. Aortic CTA demonstrated restoration of the normal anatomical relationship at the aortic root. The patient was discharged in stable condition.
Discharge diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge instructions: The patient was advised to follow-up with a primary care physician and cardiologist and adhere to medication and lifestyle modification recommendations.
label_evidence: Noncoronary SVA with mitral and aortic regurgitation, aortic aneurysm, and aortic valve stenosis with surgical repair.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted due to her underlying medical conditions including type 2 diabetes and hypertension. She also had a history of amblyopia OD and a resolved branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) in the left eye. During her hospital stay, she was treated with Eyefolate™ capsules and no further complications were reported during the course of treatment.

Clinical Progress:
In October 2013, the patient's best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/150 OD and 20/25 OS. The OS fundus photo showed a large macular aneurysm (MA) in the superior temporal region with exudates. After being prescribed the Eyefolate™ capsules, the BCVA of the left eye improved to 20/20 in August 2014. Further improvement was seen in December 2014 when the large exudates almost completely resolved in OS (Fig. b). In January 2016, the BCVA was 20/400 OD and 20/25 OS, and the MA was resolved as shown in the OS fundus photo (Fig. c) during 2016.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged in a stable condition with instructions to continue taking prescribed medications and regular follow-up appointments with her primary care physician to monitor her diabetes and hypertension. A referral to an ophthalmologist was also recommended to monitor her vision and perpetuate the effectiveness of the treatment.
label_evidence: Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, amblyopia OD, branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO)

note:
Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course: 
The patient, a 28-year-old male with moderate intellectual disability, presented with a history of comorbid diagnoses including autism spectrum disorder, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and GERD. The patient had a history of excoriation disorder, schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, and displayed symptoms of anxiety, irritability, and physical aggression. The patient was initially treated with quetiapine but was later transitioned to valbenazine due to intermittent abnormal movements. The patient's treatment was further adjusted, and clozapine was prescribed due to continued psychosis.

Hospital Stay: 
Four days after starting valbenazine treatment, improvement in abnormal movements was noted. Over two months, the patient no longer displayed any abnormal jaw movements, minimal to no arm/hand/finger movements or foot tapping, and no truncal movements. Caregivers reported that these improvements resulted in less isolating, aggressive, and confrontational behavior. The patient also became more cooperative, increasing participation in activities and displaying less resistance to caregiver assistance with activities of daily living. The patient currently remains stable on valbenazine (80 mg QHS).
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment: 
The patient was initially treated with quetiapine for symptoms of intermittent abnormal movements, which was later adjusted following persistent psychosis. Valbenazine was prescribed and later escalated to 80 mg QHS. Due to continued psychosis, clozapine was also introduced and titrated over 2 weeks to 300 mg daily.

Follow-up Plan: 
The patient is currently stable on valbenazine (80 mg QHS) with no reported adverse events. No further medication changes are planned at this time, and follow-up with the patient will continue to monitor for any changes in behavior or physical movements.
label_evidence: The patient had a history of comorbid diagnoses that included autism spectrum disorder, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and GERD. The patient also displayed symptoms of excoriation disorder, schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, anxiety, irritability, and physical aggression. Following treatment with valbenazine and clozapine, the patient displayed a significant reduction in abnormal movements and improved psychosocial behavior.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 44-year-old male
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:

The patient presented at our primary care clinic with a lump in the right nipple associated with sharp pain. The mammogram revealed a 1.2 cm mass in the right retro areolar breast. Core needle biopsy was positive for invasive ductal carcinoma ER+ and PR+ and negative for HER2-. The patient underwent simple mastectomy and right sentinel lymph node biopsy. He received dose-dense adjuvant chemotherapy which was stopped after 3 doses of Taxanes. The lymph node biopsy came back positive for metastatic carcinoma, and the patient received radiation therapy. The patient was started on Tamoxifen therapy for>5 years.

Summary:

The 44-year-old male was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma stage IIA. He underwent simple mastectomy, right sentinel lymph node biopsy, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. He was started on Tamoxifen therapy for>5 years. He denied any active complaints 3 years post diagnosis. The physical examination was positive for old healed lateral scar on the right chest. Genetic testing revealed no evidence of BRCA mutations or other evidence of familial breast cancer. The patient's annual mammographic screening and clinical exam of the contralateral breast were normal. He reported concerns of trouble maintaining erections and weight gain which were likely secondary to the effect of Tamoxifen.

Hospital course:
The patient was admitted to the CCU on [insert date] with complaints of retrosternal chest discomfort radiating to jaw, associated with nausea and diaphoresis. Based on physical examination, EKG and cardiac enzyme levels, as well as coronary angiography and TTE results, the patient was diagnosed with an acute inferior STEMI secondary to spontaneous dissection of the OM2.

Treatment:
The patient was appropriately discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy including ASA and Clopidogrel including beta blockade with Metoprolol.

Follow-up plan:
The patient was advised to continue with the prescribed medication and instructed to come for follow-up after one month.

Readmission:
One month later, the patient returned with diplopia and numbness of her left arm and face. Computed tomographic angiography showed a focal 8mm long dissection of the right vertebral artery in its V1 segment with mild associated aneurysmal dilatation. The patient was subsequently started on anticoagulation therapy to prevent future spontaneous dissections.

Discharge condition:
The patient's condition was stable at the time of discharge.

Discharge disposition:
The patient was discharged home with family members.

Follow-up plan:
The patient was advised to continue with the prescribed medication and instructed to come for follow-up after three months.
label_evidence: Acute inferior ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) secondary to spontaneous dissection of the left second obtuse marginal (OM2) coronary artery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Age: 24
Gender: Female
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital with acute pulmonary edema due to severe aortic valve insufficiency. She had previously been diagnosed with Takayasu's disease and had undergone multiple surgeries, including replacement of the distal ascending aorta and hemiarch, stenosis of celiac artery and superior mesenteric artery, and stenosis of the orifices of both renal arteries. She had a graft used to direct blood flow from the right internal iliac artery to all stenosed arteries. She also underwent a right nephrectomy due to acute thrombosis of the right renal artery graft. The patient was on steroid treatment since the diagnosis of her disease.

Treatment:
The patient underwent surgery to address the aortic valve insufficiency. The procedure was performed through a median sternotomy, and a composite graft with a mechanical valve was implanted. The patient's postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged from the hospital on the 10th postoperative day.

Follow-up:
The patient had a one year clinical follow-up that showed normal echocardiographical results, and she was doing well in normal daily activities.

Pathology:
Part of the dilated aortic root wall was sent for histological examination, which verified the diagnosis of Takayasu's arteritis.

Note:
The patient's condition was complex and required surgery to address the aortic valve insufficiency. The patient's postoperative course was uneventful, and she had a good one year clinical follow-up.
label_evidence: - Acute pulmonary edema due to severe aortic valve insufficiency - Takayasu's disease

Patient Name: Unknown

Age: 75 years

Date of Discharge: Unknown
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]Principal Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Clinical Presentation:

The patient, who had a medical history of hypertension, was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of fecal occult blood. A colonoscopy revealed a type II tumor in the sigmoid colon, which was located 23 cm from the anal verge. Histopathology of a biopsy specimen revealed moderately differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma. CT imaging showed sigmoid colon wall thickening, and regional lymph node metastasis was suspected. Blood examination showed an elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) concentration (32.7 ng/ml).

Hospital Course:

The patient underwent a laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy, which was performed without complications. Postoperative histopathological examination revealed moderately differentiated to mucinous adenocarcinoma, and three of the 16 retrieved lymph nodes contained malignant cells. The cancer was classified as stage IIIb [pT4a, pN1b, M0]. The patient was discharged after 10 days of recovery.

Treatment:

Following the diagnosis of stage III colorectal cancer, the patient was recommended to receive adjuvant chemotherapy with CAPOX starting 4 weeks after surgery. The selected regimen consisted of capecitabine and L-OHP. The anticancer drug dosage was reduced to 80% because of the patient's age. The patient also received 7.5 g of NYT daily throughout the course of adjuvant chemotherapy.

Outcome:

The patient did not report any significant adverse effects. Follow-up examination did not show any recurrence during a 1-year postoperative follow-up.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with prescribed medications and follow-up appointment schedules.

Discharge Medications:

Detailed medication list not provided in the case report.

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 18-year-old male with no significant past medical history, was admitted to the emergency department with complaints of suprapubic and periumbilical pain, accompanied by nausea for one day. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness to palpation in the periumbilical, right lower quadrant, and left upper quadrant regions. Respiratory rate, heart rate, and blood pressure were within normal limits, but complete blood count revealed leukocytosis with a left shift.

A CT exam was performed to rule out any underlying causes of the aforementioned symptoms, demonstrating a dilated and hyperenhancing retrocecal appendix containing a form of calcified materials within it. Moreover, small air collections were identified anterior to the right and left common iliac arteries, and posterior to both psoas muscles in the retroperitoneal cavity of the abdomen.

The patient was taken to the operating room for an appendectomy, during which an additional inflamed appendix, and evidence of minor perforation into the retroperitoneum were found. Surgical team continued with appendectomy in view of inferior incision area revealing no pathologic process in the retroperitoneal cavity.

The patient was monitored in the post-operative care unit and demonstrated no post-operative complications. The patient was discharged the following day in stable condition.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Instructions:

The patient is advised to take all prescribed medications and attend follow-up appointments as scheduled. Discharge instructions and the post-operative care plan have been explained to the patient in detail before being discharged.
label_evidence: The patient was diagnosed with acute appendicitis with subsequent minor perforation into the retroperitoneum.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
24-year-old female with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) presenting with multiple neck masses, fever, anemia, and profound thrombocytopenia.

Hospital Course:
The patient was initially diagnosed with CML based on bone marrow (BM) smear image, cytogenetic karyotype, and the BCR/ABL fusion transcript. She was treated with hydroxyurea and then imatinib with some success. However, she was readmitted to the hospital with multiple lymphadenopathies and progressive swelling, indicating blast crisis involving T cells. The BM showed marked hyperplasia with more than 20% blasts. The patient was treated with dasatinib and showed a significant decrease in the WBC. However, she stopped taking the medication and died two months after blast crisis treatment.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
The patient was treated with hydroxyurea, then imatinib (400mg/day), and finally, dasatinib. The dasatinib treatment showed a significant decrease in the WBC. However, the patient stopped taking the medication and died two months after blast crisis treatment.

Follow-up:
The patient died two months after blast crisis treatment.
label_evidence: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) with blast crisis involving T cells.
